power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

table.expanded: Effects were significant at both post-test (𝑑 ̅ = 1.22, 95% CI [0.952; 1.50]) and follow-up (𝑑 ̅ = 1.02, 95% CI [0.551; 1.48]), with no significant difference between assessment points (p = .272).

table.header: Overall Effects of Stepped-Care Psychological Interventions (RQ1)

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Long waiting times, fragmented care pathways, and limited access to evidence-based interventions leave many children and adolescents without appropriate treatment (Brown et al., 2002; Chavira et al., 2004; Kowalewski et al., 2011; Meng & Wiznitzer, 2024; Roennfeldt et al., 2024; Singer et al., 2022).

text.text: Stepped care aims to allocate treatment intensity according to clinical need while minimizing unnecessary use of high-intensity interventions (Bower & Gilbody, 2005).

text.text: In psychological care, stepped-care approaches typically (1) include different established and evidence-based treatments, referred to as steps, varying in their intensity (e.g., treatment continuum starting with low-intensity, low-barrier, and cost-effective treatments transitioning to more intensive and often more costly treatments) and (2) define specific criteria for when individuals transition between the different steps (e.g., non-response within a specific time frame and/or individual preference) (Bower & Gilbody, 2005).

text.text: When applied to individuals at elevated risk or with subthreshold symptoms, these approaches are often described as preventive stepped care, whereas models targeting diagnosed mental disorders are typically referred to as stepped-care treatments.

Notably, school-based service models such as multi-tiered systems of support (MTSS, e.g., Arora et al., 2019; Lee & Gage, 2020; Sugai & Horner, 2009) follow principles closely aligned with stepped care by matching support intensity to student needs across tiers.
text.formatted: Notably, school-based service models such as multi-tiered systems of support (MTSS, e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Arora et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Lee & Gage, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Sugai & Horner, 2009)</ref> follow principles closely aligned with stepped care by matching support intensity to student needs across tiers.

text.text: However, these frameworks typically use different terminology and are often implemented at the school level rather than through predefined individual transition criteria.
Two broad stepped-care approaches are commonly distinguished.
In progressive stepped care, all patients start with the lowest step and transition to more intense steps, if needed.

In stratified stepped-care models, patients are assigned to an intervention to which they are individually more likely to respond, with the possibility of increasing treatment intensity when responding insufficiently with lower-level care (Arns et al., 2022; Asarnow et al., 2025).

text.text: Proceeding from this rationale, general models of care can also be offered in a stepped format.
For example, collaborative, or shared care can also be stepped (Härter et al., 2018) to aid in a smooth transition across the continuum of interventions.

text.text: Across both approaches, stepped-care models are intended to improve efficiency, accessibility, and coordination of mental healthcare services by reserving more resource-intensive interventions for children and youths requiring additional support.

Although stepped-care models have been investigated across a wide range of mental health conditions, including personality disorders (Grenyer & Bailey, 2024), depression (Jagayat et al., 2024), anxiety (Wuthrich et al., 2021), PTSD (Roberts & Nixon, 2023), substance abuse (Morse et al., 2023), eating disorders (Le Grange et al., 2021), insomnia (Schlarb et al., 2025), and have also been combined with transdiagnostic treatments targeting shared psychological processes (Kennedy et al., 2021), their implementation in routine practice remains challenging (Hermens et al., 2014; Marchionatti et al., 2024; Richards et al., 2012).

text.text: In particular, uncertainty persists regarding which interventions should be included as treatment steps, how transitions between steps should be determined, and to what extent current stepped-care implementations reflect the principle of beginning with low-intensity and scalable interventions (e.g., Berger et al., 2022; Hermens et al., 2014).

text.text: These challenges may be especially relevant in child and adolescent mental health systems, where developmental considerations, caregiver involvement, school contexts, and concerns regarding risk management may complicate treatment allocation and monitoring.
In sum, evidence from adult stepped-care systems may not generalize directly to children and adolescents due to differences in development and contexts of implementation.

Previous reviews have identified substantial variation in the structure and intensity of interventions included within stepped-care models, ranging from watchful waiting and self-help interventions to individual psychotherapy and intensive care services.
The steps can be ordered based on various criteria.

text.text: In light of the growing interest in stepped care as a scalable model for child and adolescent mental health services, this meta-analysis provides timely evidence to guide researchers, practitioners, and policymakers.

Existing reviews have primarily focused on clinical effectiveness within specific disorders or adult populations, with less attention to implementation characteristics, transition procedures, and scalability in child and adolescent mental health systems.

Studies were included in the current meta-analysis when they fulfilled all the following three criteria: 1.
In the study, a stepped-care psychological intervention was implemented.

The stepped-care intervention (1) explicitly included at least two predefined intervention components (i.e., steps), (2) varied in intensity and patient burden according to the patient needs, and (3) implemented predefined and explicit criteria to transition between steps (e.g., non-response after eight weeks).
The participants were children and adolescents ranging from 0-21 years of age.

The study reported (a) a percentage regarding dropout, response, remission, or number of participants transitioning to the next step and/or (b) a standardized effect size with the corresponding number of participants or descriptive data (e.g., means, standard deviations, and number of participants).
The effect size can relate either to pre-post within-group effects or post-post comparisons across two different groups (e.g., stepped care CBT vs.
CBT).

We included studies independent of the control condition (e.g., no control, passive control, active control), the reported outcome (e.g., response, remission, quality of life, costs), and the characteristics of the stepped-care intervention (e.g., number of steps, stepping up or down criteria, and progressive or stratified stepped care).
Relevant studies were identified through two distinct search procedures, a standardized search and an exploratory hand search.

For the standardized search, we searched titles and abstracts (PsycInfo, Medline) or titles, abstracts, and keywords (CENTRAL) for papers published from the database inception to October 2026, limited to "Human," "English language" (all three databases).

We used the same standardized search string that included commonly used keywords regarding the stepped-care intervention (first bracket) and the age group (second bracket) for each database: (stepped care or sequential treatment* or adjunctive treatment* or tier* treatment* or adaptive treatment* or staged treatment* or sequential intervention* or adjunctive intervention* or tier* intervention* or adaptive intervention* or staged intervention* or sequential psycho* or adjunctive psycho* or tier* psycho* or adaptive psycho* or staged psycho*) and (adolescent* or teen* or young people or youth* or child*)

For the exploratory search, we screened the references of the included studies of all published meta-analyses on steppedcare psychological interventions (Firth et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2016; Rivero-Santana et al., 2021; van Straten et al., 2015) and reviews on stepped-care interventions in children and adolescents (Berger et al., 2022; Kendall et al., 2016; Ollendick et al., 2018).

text.text: Coding occurred in a two-step procedure.
In the first step, all 2,358 abstracts were screened for inclusion.
The inclusion criteria were liberally applied to minimize the chance of falsely excluding relevant articles based on the title and abstract.
Two trained and independent raters screened half of the titles and abstracts for inclusion.
Their inter-rater agreement for the inclusion of studies based on titles and abstracts was high with 98%; Cohen's κ = .825.
Coder A then rated the remaining half of the identified hits.
If either of the two coders included the reference based on the title and abstract screening, the full text was assessed for eligibility.
A total of 113 full texts (88 from the standardized search, 25 from the exploratory search) were obtained for further investigation.
In the second step, the full texts of all relevant abstracts were screened for inclusion and exclusion and coded.
The same two raters independently screened all full texts for inclusion in the meta-analysis.
The inter-rater agreement for the inclusion of the full texts was 89%, Cohen's κ = .805.
Again, disagreements were resolved through discussion.

text.text: Cost outcomes were restricted to intervention costs, when studies reported total health care or societal costs, which include costs not directly attributable to the intervention, only the intervention cost component was coded.
Quality-adjusted life years reported in economic evaluations were not coded, as they combine utility scores with time.
For sequential multiple assignment randomized trials (SMARTs), all embedded intervention sequences consisted of predefined steps with explicit transition criteria.

Effects were coded as reported, typically pooled across second-stage options within first-stage conditions; as SMARTs compared different stepped-care sequences rather than stepped care versus a control condition, they contributed pre-post and proportional data but no controlled effects.
Whether the design was a SMART was examined as a moderator.
The mean inter-rater agreement across all variables was 89%; for categorical variables the mean Cohen's κ was .787.
Whenever relevant data regarding the effect size were missing from the original article, we contacted the authors requesting the missing data.
In total, we contacted seven authors, four of whom responded to our request.

We performed two types of meta-analyses: (1) a meta-analysis for standardized mean differences of within effects (i.e., pre-post effects) or group differences (i.e., post-post or pre-post gain group differences), and (2) a meta-analysis for proportional data (i.e., proportion that transitioned, dropout, response, and remission).

Transition was defined as the proportion of participants who moved from one step to the next according to the study-specific transition criteria (e.g., clinical non-response or patient/family request).
The data preparation was twofold.
For within and between effects, we computed the effect size as Cohen's d from the coded descriptive data using syntax.
For 55 effect sizes, descriptive data were not available.
Instead, we converted the reported chi 2 (k = 18) or odds ratio from the contingency table (k = 29) using syntax.
In two cases, we had to apply continuity correction at the 2 × 2 contingency table, since two cells were 0 (Salloum et al., 2016; Wainer et al., 2021).

text.text: The 50 studies included data from 39 independent samples comprising 4,007 participants.
The samples' mean ages ranged from 3.15 years to 17.40 years and included participants between 1 and 21 years.
The most reported effect sizes related to PTSS/PTSD (26%), followed by anxiety disorders (23%), and obsessive-compulsive disorder (11%).
Furthermore, many effect sizes were from studies conducted in the United States (43%), followed by Australia (16%) and Sweden (11%).

Of all reported effect sizes, 108 related to proportions from 36 independent samples reported in 39 studies (i.e., proportions on transition, response, remission, dropout), 195 to uncontrolled effects from 25 independent samples reported in 31 studies (i.e., pre-post effects, various outcomes), and 167 to controlled effects from 15 independent samples reported in 18 studies (i.e., group differences from controlled trials or randomized controlled trials, various outcomes).
For the controlled trials, most reported effects compared stepped-care interventions to active controls.

In 12 of 15 independent samples (80%), the control condition consisted of the full-dose version of the most intensive step of the respective steppedcare intervention, delivered to all participants from the outset.
Two samples compared stepped care with usual care, and one with a passive control.
The reported proportions ranged from .063 to .990, the pre-post effect from d = -1.15 to d = 4.80, and the controlled effects from d = -1.50 to d = 2.58.

The overall pre-post effect for uncontrolled studies, summarizing 195 effect sizes from 25 unique samples, demonstrates a significant positive effect of stepped-care interventions with 𝑑 ̅ = 1.25, 95% CI [0.982; 1.51].
We found no evidence of moderation for sample characteristics such as age or gender.
Furthermore, stepped-care interventions significantly reduced symptoms (𝑑 ̅ = 1.41, 95% CI [1.11; 1.71]) and significantly enhanced functioning (𝑑 ̅ = 0.814, 95% CI [0.439; 1.19]).
Effects on parent/family outcomes were available for only three samples and, as such, not summarized.
Effects were significant at both post-test (𝑑 ̅ = 1.22, 95% CI [0.952; 1.50]) and follow-up (𝑑 ̅ = 1.02, 95% CI [0.551; 1.48]), with no significant difference between assessment points (p = .272).

Regarding assessment source, pre-post effects were significant for self-reports (𝑑 ̅ = 0.840, 95% CI [0.585; 1.10]), parent reports (𝑑 ̅ = 1.02, 95% CI [0.846; 1.20]), clinician ratings (𝑑 ̅ = 1.56, 95% CI [1.07; 2.04]), and mixed sources (𝑑 ̅ = 2.05, 95% CI [1.36; 2.74]), while the assessment source significantly moderated the effect (p = .025).
Teacher reports were available for only one sample.

Overall, the results demonstrate significant pre-post effects of stepped-care interventions; apart from assessment source, there was no evidence of moderation by sample, outcome, or methodological characteristics (see Table 1, left columns for detailed results).

text.text: The overall effect of stepped care when compared to a control group (i.e., post-post group differences or group differences in pre-post gains) summarizing 167 effect sizes from 15 unique samples indicates no significant difference across groups, with 𝑑 ̅ = 0.039, 95% CI [-0.162; 0.240].
The estimate was similar when restricted to randomized controlled trials (𝑑 ̅ = -0.019, 95% CI [-0.224; 0.186]) while only two samples came from non-randomized controlled trials.
Effects did not differ by effect size type (post-post: 𝑑 ̅ = 0.089, 95% CI [-0.129; 0.307]; pre-post gain: 𝑑 ̅ = 0.021, 95% CI [-0.114; 0.157]; p = .856).
As almost all samples used active controls, the type of control condition could not be tested.
The same applied to blinding.

Regarding outcomes, none of the clinical outcome categories showed a significant difference between stepped care and control conditions: symptoms (𝑑 ̅ = 0.038, 95% CI [-0.094; 0.171]), remission (𝑑 ̅ = -0.271, 95% CI [-0.628; 0.086]), functioning (𝑑 ̅ = -0.020, 95% CI [-0.143; 0.104]), dropout (𝑑 ̅ = -0.165, 95% CI [-0.669; 0.338]), and treatment satisfaction (𝑑 ̅ = -0.116, 95% CI [-0.447; 0.216]).
Intervention costs were significantly lower for stepped care (𝑑 ̅ = 1.23, 95% CI [0.213; 2.24]); given the small number of samples, this estimate should be considered preliminary.
Two studies additionally reported total health care and societal costs, which include costs beyond intervention delivery (e.g., other health services, productivity losses).
Descriptively, total costs were lower in the stepped-care groups in both studies; the difference was significant in Aspvall, Sampaio, et al. (2021) but not in Chatterton et al. (2019).

Effects did not vary by assessment source (p = .734).

text.text: For both the pre-post effects of stepped-care interventions and the between-group effects in controlled trials, we did not identify any significant moderator relating to the intervention characteristics.

The effectiveness did not vary by intervention aim (pre-post: p = .706; controlled: p = .365), the number of steps (pre-post: p = .092), overall duration of treatment (pre-post: p = .826, controlled: p = .365), the target population addressed (pre-post: p = .493; controlled: p = .398), the professionals involved (pre-post: p = .582), whether psychopharmacotherapy was included or not (pre-post: p = .980), the timing of the first decision point (pre-post: p = .202), or shared decision-making (pre-post: p = .063).
Because of the small number of studies, we could not statistically test differences based on the professionals involved and the number of steps for controlled effects.

This meta-analysis integrated available evidence on stepped-care psychological interventions for children and adolescents, with the aims of assessing overall effectiveness, exploring potential moderators of treatment effects, informing clinical implementation, and identifying priorities for future research.
The findings yielded three key insights.
First, stepped care did not differ significantly from control conditions in clinical outcomes, although controls mostly received the fulldose version of the most intensive step.
Preliminary evidence further suggests lower intervention costs.
Second, approximately half of the patients did not transition beyond the initial step, which was of lower intensity relative to subsequent steps.

Third, stepped-care models varied substantially in their aims, implemented steps, and transition criteria, whereas genuinely low-intensity initial steps, multi-informant transition criteria, and settings with broader reach were rarely implemented.

The present findings indicate that stepped-care interventions did not differ significantly in clinical outcomes from control conditions, which in most studies consisted of the full-dose version of the most intensive stepped-care step delivered to all participants from the outset, while being associated with lower intervention costs in the small number of studies reporting cost data.
We found significant pre-post effects of stepped-care interventions for outcomes regarding symptoms and functioning.
Furthermore, the pre-post effects persisted up to the follow-up assessments.
Descriptively, positive effects were found across various mental disorders.
The positive pre-post effects (𝑑 ̅ = 1.25) are comparable in direction and magnitude to previous meta-analytic findings on the effects of stepped care in adult patients (Wakefield et al., 2021).

text.text: The current meta-analysis included a younger age group and a broader range of mental disorders and outcomes, which might serve as a potential explanation.
Furthermore, the control conditions in the current meta-analysis included full-dose treatments in relation to the stepped-care intervention in most cases.
The effects of stepped-care interventions might be even higher in magnitude when compared to care involving waiting-list controls.
Approximately half of the patients who completed the first step did not transition to a subsequent step.
As transition criteria were mostly based on clinical response, this suggests that the initial step was sufficient for a substantial proportion of patients.
However, non-transition may also reflect natural recovery or treatment dropout, and should therefore not be equated with treatment success.
Moreover, it is important to note that the initial steps were of lower intensity only relative to subsequent steps.

Treatment intensity can be reduced along several dimensions, including the type and format of treatment (e.g., self-help or digital instead of face-to-face therapy), the dose (e.g., number and length of sessions), and the degree and qualification of professional involvement (e.g., guided self-help or lay counsellors instead of therapist-led treatment).

In most included studies, the initial step was reduced on only one or two of these dimensions and frequently consisted of structured, professionally delivered treatment (e.g., individual CBT with fewer sessions or internet-delivered CBT with therapist guidance), which may itself be considered moderate-to high-intensity care.

Accordingly, our findings indicate that a less intensive start than the full-dose treatment did not compromise outcomes, but they do not speak to the effectiveness of genuinely low-intensity first steps, such as self-directed interventions or single-session interventions, which were rarely implemented.

The finding highlights the potential of stepped-care models to reduce unnecessary exposure to more intensive and costly treatments while preserving opportunities for escalation when clinically indicated.
However, evidence regarding optimal criteria for selecting initial treatment intensity and determining transitions between steps remains limited.

Most studies based transition decisions primarily on disorder-specific, mostly clinician-rated symptom measures, whereas functioning and patient preferences were rarely considered, and only a minority of studies used shared decision-making.
Our findings suggest that two distinct decisions should be distinguished.
First, the decision whether a transition is clinically indicated should be based on standardized outcome monitoring (McAleavey et al., 2024).

Second, the decision to which step a patient should transition may benefit from shared decision-making with young people and their families, as proposed in stratified stepped-care models.
Accommodating patient preferences has been associated with lower dropout and better outcomes in psychotherapy (e.g., Swift & Callahan, 2009; von Wirth et al., 2025; Wasmann et al., 2019).

text.text: As the moderation by assessment source was observed only in uncontrolled pre-post comparisons, these implications should be tested in future research.
A central finding of this review was the substantial heterogeneity in how stepped-care interventions were implemented across studies.

Although stepped-care models are typically conceptualized as beginning with low-intensity, scalable interventions that are intensified only when needed, many included studies implemented relatively intensive initial treatment steps.

This pattern suggests a potential implementation paradox in child and adolescent mental health care: stepped care aims for scalability and efficiency, yet its implementation frequently relies on resource-intensive intervention pathways.
Notably, genuinely low-intensity interventions have been found to be effective in prior research.

For example, single-session interventions (SSI), defined as interventions that intentionally involve only one visit or encounter with a clinic or healthcare provider (Schleider et al., 2020), have demonstrated good effectiveness for a variety of patients of various age groups and mental disorders (Schleider et al., 2025).

text.text: Extending the steps by scalable, stigma-free, and low-barrier interventions, such as self-directed SSIs, can be a valuable extension of stepped-care approaches.
Several factors may contribute to the limited use of low-intensity interventions.

Clinicians and services may have concerns regarding risk management, symptom complexity, family involvement, and the developmental appropriateness of minimally guided interventions for younger populations and may be unfamiliar with the approach itself (e.g., Berger et al., 2022; Franx et al., 2012).

text.text: In addition, strained patient relationships, reimbursement structures, limited availability of resources and validated low-intensity interventions, and implementation barriers in school or community settings may constrain adoption (e.g., Brantnell et al., 2026; Heath et al., 2026; Maehder et al., 2020).

text.text: Consequently, some interventions labeled as stepped care may more closely resemble treatment sequencing or resource triage models than fully progressive stepped-care systems.
Furthermore, developmental considerations may distinguish stepped-care implementation in children and youth and adult mental health systems.

Treatment transitions in children and youth services often involve caregivers, schools, and multidisciplinary providers, while symptom presentation and treatment needs may vary considerably across developmental stages.
These factors may complicate decisions regarding treatment intensity and modality, monitoring, and transition.
Moreover, only one of the included studies has used a stratified stepped-care approach to decide on the initial step and subsequent transition (Olsson et al., 2025).

text.text: However, empirical evidence is scarce, especially for children and youth.

Initial findings indicate that stratified stepped care may yield better outcomes than care as usual in youth and young adults (Asarnow et al., 2025), and a pilot trial suggested advantages over progressive stepped care (Olsson et al., 2025).

text.text: Nonetheless, further research is needed to directly compare different stepped-care models and establish their relative effectiveness.
As with other meta-analyses, this review is not without limitations.

First, almost all control conditions included patients receiving the full-dose version of the most intensive step of the stepped-care group, usually treatments currently delivered in contemporary health systems, as a comparator to the stepped-care group.
However, it is unclear whether stepped-care models have further benefits, such as reducing treatment barriers, waiting times and buffering the associated increase in symptoms.

Comparing stepped-care interventions with care as usual when entering the health system involving long waiting times might provide further insights into the potential benefits of stepped-care treatments.
Second, the number of studies in some of the moderator categories was rather low (i.e., fewer than five).
While the meta-analytic results are not fully reliable in these cases, they indicate relevant gaps in the research that can be investigated in future studies.
For example, we were unable to determine possible moderating effects due to intervention characteristics, such as the number of steps or using a shared decision-making approach.

Further, not much is known about the mechanisms specific to stepped care, such as the possible synergistic effects of the different steps, as proposed and identified in previous research (Cornish & Berry, 2025; Tobias et al., 2022).

Third, most effect sizes were derived from studies conducted with WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) samples within mental health care systems.
Only a few studies have included non-WEIRD samples, for example from Brazil (Fatori et al., 2018) or India (Malik et al., 2022).

text.text: Fourth, most stepped-care interventions were initiated in specialist mental health outpatient settings, whereas relatively few began in schools, community services, or general medical settings such as emergency departments, although these settings may be particularly suited for low-threshold initial steps.

A recent review showed that low-intensity interventions delivered in school settings are effective (Cohen et al., 2024), suggesting that schools may be a promising setting for the initial step of stepped-care models.

School-based tiered support models, such as multi-tiered systems of support (MTSS), use different terminology and may therefore be underrepresented in the current review.

Moreover, these models are rarely labeled as stepped care, research has largely examined school-wide implementation or individual tiers in isolation (e.g., Cho Blair et al., 2021; Lee & Gage, 2020), and transitions are often based on triage processes rather than a predefined sequence of steps increasing in intensity.

By integrating effectiveness and implementation findings, this review aims to address important gaps in the current literature and inform the development of stepped-care approaches in routine clinical practice.

RQ2: Are the effects of stepped-care interventions moderated by characteristics of the stepped-care approach?
RQ3: Which steps are implemented in stepped-care psychological interventions for children and adolescents?

Given the worldwide increasing demand for mental health services, future stepped-care research may particularly benefit from integrating digital interventions, school-based services, and precision mental health approaches to improve scalability and accessibility across diverse cultural backgrounds and mental health care settings.ConclusionsIn sum, stepped-care interventions for children and adolescents were associated with large improvements from pre-to post-treatment across various mental health problems.
In controlled trials, stepped care did not differ significantly from control conditions in clinical outcomes.

As these controls mostly received the full-dose version of the most intensive step from the outset, the findings indicate that starting with a less intensive step did not compromise clinical outcomes.
Preliminary evidence from a small number of studies further suggests lower intervention costs.

At the same time, most stepped-care models combined two relatively intensive steps, were initiated in specialist mental health services, and based transition decisions primarily on clinician-rated, disorder-specific symptom measures.
Genuinely low-intensity, scalable initial steps, multi-informant transition criteria, and shared decision-making were rarely implemented.

Given constrained mental health resources and the rising number of children and adolescents seeking care, stepped care is a promising service delivery model, but its potential to increase reach and efficiency remains largely untested.

Future research should evaluate low-intensity initial steps, such as single-session or digital interventions, compare stepped care with routine care pathways that involve waiting times, and examine implementation in settings with broader reach, such as schools, primary care, and emergency departments.
